strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: text-driven generation of navigable, multi-room 3D environments, where existing image/video-prior methods often fail to maintain long-range spatial and object consistency.

The geometry-first decomposition is compelling as an Applied/Systems contribution: using an explicit mesh scaffold for layout, object placement, texture propagation, mesh-conditioned image generation, validation, and 3DGS reconstruction is a coherent system design rather than a single new algorithm. Judged on that basis, the contribution is meaningful.

The qualitative results are visually strong, especially for close-up object rotations and room-to-room transitions, and the ablations are useful: depth-only, depth+objects, depth+walls+bboxes, and full conditioning isolate the value of object geometry and accumulated structural textures.

The paper compares against a broad set of relevant baselines, including panorama-to-3D, autoregressive world generation, iterative lifting, and layout-guided generation. The user study directly targets the main claim of improved 3D object and structure consistency.

The method description is generally clear, with helpful implementation details in the appendix, including camera placement, texture accumulation, object placement heuristics, prompts, and baseline setup.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. The system depends on several proprietary or difficult-to-access components, including Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects, and key model choices appear to be selected empirically. This makes independent reproduction and fair comparison difficult.

The appendix reveals that object segmentation uses interactive point-based SAM3 annotation by a user, whereas the main method reads like an automatic text-to-3D pipeline. This manual step is substantial because object masks determine the scaffold objects, and it weakens the claim of end-to-end text-driven generation unless automation quality is demonstrated.

The evaluation does not fully substantiate the strongest claims about arbitrary scale and multi-room generation. Baseline comparisons are mostly framed around single-room or local trajectories because many baselines cannot handle multi-room scenes, while the paper’s central novelty is environment-scale multi-room synthesis. There are no scaling experiments over number of rooms, runtime/memory analysis, failure rates, or quantitative layout/geometry consistency metrics across rooms.

The user study is promising but underspecified: the number of scenes, prompts, videos per method, randomization details, statistical significance, and participant screening are not sufficiently reported in the main paper. The very high pairwise preference rates may be real, but the protocol needs more detail to rule out presentation or selection bias.

Baseline adaptation may favor the proposed method. For example, SpatialGen receives the authors’ generated scaffold/layout, while other methods are constrained by their native input assumptions; it is unclear whether all baselines were tuned comparably or evaluated on trajectories equally favorable/unfavorable to them.

Several claims are overstated. The paper claims scalable or arbitrarily-sized generation and robust 3D consistency, but the method still relies on per-view image synthesis, heuristic validation, regenerated seeds, manual segmentation, and 3DGS optimization from synthesized images. These components can fail silently or accumulate appearance inconsistencies.

The image verification step checks recall of mesh depth edges from monocular estimated depth, but it ignores false positives and allows the image model to add plausible objects not present in the scaffold. This may preserve major structure while still permitting view-dependent hallucinations that harm 3D consistency.

The limitations section is too narrow. It mentions single-story layouts and SAM-3D occlusion artifacts, but should also discuss manual interaction, dependence on closed models/APIs, computational cost, prompt sensitivity, licensing/attribution of generated assets, and failure modes for complex topology or dense clutter.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: scalable, navigable, multi-room 3D scene generation from language prompts, where current image/video-prior methods often suffer from drift and poor view consistency.

The geometry-first decomposition is sensible. Using a mesh scaffold for structural layout, object placement, view-conditioned image generation, and depth-regularized 3DGS reconstruction is a coherent systems idea that addresses a real weakness of purely pixel-space pipelines.

The manuscript is generally clear about the high-level pipeline and includes useful ablations showing that depth alone, objects alone, and wall texture cues contribute differently to multi-view consistency.

The qualitative examples and user-study numbers, if taken at face value, suggest the method can produce visually appealing scenes with better close-view object consistency than several recent baselines.
weaknesses: The claimed text-to-3D automation is substantially undermined by the appendix: object segmentation uses SAM3 in interactive point-based mode with user-provided positive/negative clicks and labels. This is a major hidden human-in-the-loop component, not a minor implementation detail, and it directly affects object richness, placement, and final quality.

Reproducibility is poor. The pipeline relies on proprietary or difficult-to-access components including Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects. Key prompts, seeds, runtime/cost, rejection rates for validation, number of generated/regenerated views, and implementation details are incomplete, making independent verification unlikely.

The contribution is mostly a system integration of existing LLMs, image generators, segmenters, object reconstruction models, and 3DGS. The paper does not introduce a strong new algorithmic component, and the novelty over layout-guided/scaffold-guided generation is incremental relative to the scale of the claims.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing. The user study lacks crucial details such as the number of scenes/prompts, exact comparison protocol, participant calibration, statistical significance, whether videos were matched in trajectory and duration, and whether outputs were cherry-picked. The extremely high pairwise preferences, including 100% over some baselines, raise concerns without stronger protocol transparency.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or under-specified. Several baselines are designed for different input assumptions or single-room/panorama settings, while the proposed method benefits from a generated scaffold, manual object annotation, and proprietary image-editing APIs. SpatialGen is given the authors’ generated layout/object locations, but the comparison does not clearly isolate method capability from input advantage.
The ablation study is narrow: it is conducted on a single six-room gothic mansion layout, so it does not establish robustness across scene types, layouts, or object densities.

The method’s actual limitations are much broader than stated. Besides single-story layouts and object-backface issues, it depends on rectangular-ish rooms/camera heuristics, manual annotation, API model behavior, depth-edge validation that ignores false positives, and object reconstructions that may not be physically correct or complete.

The paper makes strong claims such as scalable, arbitrarily-sized, environment-scale generation, but provides little quantitative evidence on scaling behavior, memory/time costs, failure rates, maximum scene size, or degradation with increasing number of rooms.

Some design choices are questionable or internally inconsistent. The validation metric only checks recall of scaffold depth edges and explicitly ignores extra geometry, while the prompt asks the image model not to add/remove/rearrange objects; this leaves room for hallucinated appearance and geometry that could still pass validation.

Given the hidden manual intervention, weak reproducibility, and insufficiently rigorous evaluation, the paper does not yet make a convincing scientific case for ECCV acceptance despite an appealing problem and plausible qualitative outputs.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: text-conditioned generation of navigable, multi-room 3D environments rather than isolated objects or single-room scenes. The geometry-first decomposition into a generated mesh scaffold, mesh-conditioned image synthesis, validation, and geometry-regularized 3DGS is well motivated and addresses real failure modes of pixel-space scene expansion methods.

The method is technically coherent. Explicit room layout geometry, reconstructed object meshes, progressive texture accumulation, and depth-regularized 3DGS form a plausible pipeline for improving both local object consistency and global spatial coherence.

The qualitative results are compelling, especially for close-up object rotations and transitions across rooms, where many existing image/video prior methods tend to drift. The ablations in Table 2 and Figure 5 support the central claim that depth, textured walls, and object geometry are complementary conditioning signals.

The experimental section compares against a broad set of relevant recent baselines, including panorama-to-3D, iterative T2I lifting, video-diffusion world generation, and layout-guided scene generation. The perceptual study results strongly favor WorldMesh across object consistency, structure consistency, and overall quality.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with useful implementation details in the appendix, including conditioning prompts, object placement details, and baseline setup.
weaknesses: A major concern is that the claimed text-to-3D automation is weakened by the appendix: object segmentation uses interactive point-based SAM3 with user-provided positive and negative clicks. This manual intervention is central to object instantiation but is not clearly reflected in the main method or claims. The suggested VLM automation is not evaluated.

Reproducibility is limited because the pipeline depends on several proprietary, unreleased, or API-based components, including Claude Opus 4.6, Flux2-Klein, Nano Banana Pro, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects. The paper does not provide enough information on prompts, seeds, failure rates, regeneration counts, runtime, API costs, or implementation details to make the full system independently reproducible.

The quantitative evaluation is promising but not fully rigorous. The user study reports 31 participants but gives limited detail on the number of scenes, clips, trials per method, statistical significance, confidence intervals, or inter-rater variability. The very high pairwise preference rates would be more convincing with a clearer protocol and uncertainty estimates.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat difficult to interpret because many baselines are not designed for multi-room generation, while the shown comparison focuses on one room within WorldMesh outputs. This is reasonable for establishing current limitations, but the paper should more carefully separate single-room quality, multi-room scalability, and navigability claims.

The method appears to require substantial pipeline engineering and external model orchestration, yet runtime, memory beyond the GPU used, number of generated images, regeneration frequency, and total wall-clock cost are not reported. These details matter for an applied/systems-style contribution.

The generated geometry is still constrained to single-story indoor layouts, and object quality depends on single-view reconstruction, which can yield incomplete backs or missing occluded details. These limitations are acknowledged, but their practical impact is not quantified.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem: generating navigable, multi-room 3D environments from text, where purely image/video-based methods often drift geometrically. The explicit mesh-scaffold formulation is a sensible and well-motivated systems contribution for separating global structure from local photorealistic appearance.

The proposed pipeline is technically coherent: LLM-generated floor plans are converted into structural meshes, image synthesis supplies object layouts, SAM/SAM-3D reconstructs object geometry, mesh renderings condition iterative view generation, and depth-regularized 3DGS produces the final navigable scene.

The experimental section includes several relevant baselines across panorama-to-3D, autoregressive world generation, layout-guided generation, and iterative T2I lifting. The qualitative comparisons, ablations, user study, scaling table, and local/proprietary backbone comparison provide a broader evidence package than many generative-scene papers.

The ablations are useful and support the core design choices: reconstructed objects, wall texture accumulation, mesh-conditioned 3DGS initialization, and mesh depth loss all contribute to consistency. The fully local Flux2-klein variant is also a valuable attempt to separate the scaffold contribution from reliance on one commercial image model.

The paper is generally clear and gives many implementation details, including camera sampling, validation, prompts, baseline setup, runtime/cost scaling, and limitations. The approach is best viewed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one, and under that lens the integration is meaningful.
weaknesses: The degree of automation is weaker than the main text's text-to-3D framing suggests. Object masks are obtained interactively with point prompts in SAM3, and the appendix only states that this could alternatively be automated. This is a substantial reproducibility and scalability concern because object selection/segmentation can strongly affect scene quality.

The strongest reported results depend on multiple very recent or proprietary foundation models, especially Nano Banana Pro and Claude Opus 4.6. Although a local Flux2-klein variant is reported, it performs noticeably worse on consistency and quality, so the headline results may be hard to reproduce or compare fairly without API access and model/version stability.

The novelty is primarily an engineering composition of existing components rather than a new generative model or deeply novel optimization method. The mesh-conditioning idea is compelling, but many ingredients are inherited from LLM layout generation, ControlNet-like conditioning, SAM/SAM-3D, projective texturing, and 3DGS depth regularization.

The evaluation remains limited relative to the broad claims of scalable, arbitrarily sized, environment-scale generation. Quantitative consistency is computed over only five multi-room scenes, the perceptual ablation uses a single scene, and the user study details lack statistical analysis, confidence intervals, participant expertise, and controls for prompt/trajectory selection.

Some metrics are partly self-referential or incomplete. Mesh alignment is only available for the proposed method and measures agreement with its own scaffold rather than semantic or perceptual correctness. CLIP-IQA and aesthetic scores do not establish 3D consistency, and the reprojection metric may not capture object identity preservation or physically plausible geometry.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully balanced. Several baselines are designed for single-room, panorama-centered, or predefined-trajectory settings, while WorldMesh is evaluated with a scaffold tailored to the desired scene and, for SpatialGen, uses inputs derived from the proposed pipeline. This makes the gap plausible but not entirely clean as an apples-to-apples comparison.

The method has practical limitations beyond the short limitations paragraph: single-story layouts, dependence on accurate object reconstruction, incomplete/occluded back faces, possible accumulated texture errors, high per-scene generation time, view rejection/yield issues, and uncertain behavior for cluttered, non-Manhattan, outdoor, dynamic, or semantically constrained environments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: scalable, navigable multi-room 3D scene generation from text, where current image/video-prior methods often struggle with long-range consistency.

The core systems idea of using an explicit mesh scaffold as persistent geometry for conditioning image synthesis is sensible and well motivated. The pipeline addresses both global layout and local object consistency, rather than optimizing only for attractive 2D views.

The qualitative examples and ablations suggest that depth, object meshes, wall texture accumulation, and mesh-regularized 3DGS each contribute to consistency, especially compared with depth-only or bounding-box variants.

The manuscript is generally readable and includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including camera sampling, validation, object placement heuristics, cost/scaling tables, and navigability analysis.
weaknesses: The contribution is better viewed as an Applied/Systems pipeline rather than a new algorithmic advance. Under that lens, reproducibility and evidence become central, but the system depends heavily on proprietary or unreleased components such as Claude Opus 4.6, Nano Banana Pro, Flux2-Klein, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects. This makes the reported results hard to reproduce or fairly attribute to the proposed scaffold design rather than to closed foundation models.

A major concern is manual intervention: the object segmentation stage uses interactive SAM3 point prompts per object. This weakens the claim of text-to-3D scene generation and makes comparisons to automated baselines potentially unfair unless the amount of human input is quantified and matched or ablated.

The evaluation is too limited for the scale of the claims. Quantitative 3D-consistency results are over only five scenes, the perceptual ablation is on a single scene, and there is little reporting of variance, statistical significance, number of videos/ratings per condition, participant filtering, or whether scenes were cherry-picked.

The baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Several baselines are designed for single-room, panorama, or trajectory-specific settings, while WorldMesh is given generated layouts, object reconstruction, manual masks, and mesh conditioning. The paper acknowledges this mismatch but still makes strong superiority claims.

The automatic metrics are insufficiently justified. CLIP-IQA and aesthetic scores are weak proxies for 3D scene quality, while the depth reprojection and mesh-alignment metrics depend on estimated depth and/or the authors' own scaffold. It is unclear how well these metrics capture true geometric correctness rather than agreement with the pipeline's priors.

The claimed scalability to 'arbitrarily large' environments is overstated. Experiments cover up to 12 single-story rooms, with single-story layouts only, 24 views per room, nontrivial reseeding, and substantial runtime. The method also assumes relatively regular indoor room structure and does not demonstrate robustness to complex topology, stairs, outdoor spaces, or functional constraints.

The method description leaves important engineering details underspecified, including thresholds for accepting generated images, failure/retry rates beyond aggregate yield, how manual object labels are chosen, how cross-room style consistency is enforced, and how invalid LLM layouts are handled in difficult prompts.

Some results appear visually promising, but the paper does not provide enough failure analysis. Known issues such as incomplete object backs, texture seams, hallucinated fine details, inconsistent lighting, and occluded geometry are mentioned only briefly despite being central to whether the generated scenes are truly navigable and 3D consistent.

The novelty is incremental at the conceptual level: combine LLM layout generation, scaffold mesh rendering, image-conditioned diffusion, object reconstruction, projective texturing, and 3DGS with depth regularization. This is a reasonable integration, but the paper does not isolate a sufficiently original technical mechanism to offset the reproducibility and evaluation weaknesses.

strengths: This is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic paper: the main value is a well-engineered pipeline that combines LLM-based floor plans, explicit mesh scaffolds, object reconstruction, mesh-conditioned diffusion, validation, and geometry-regularized 3DGS. Under that framing, the contribution is significant and relevant to environment-scale 3D generation.

The central idea of using a persistent scaffold mesh to separate global structure from local photorealistic appearance is compelling. It directly addresses a real limitation of pixel/video-only world generation: view drift and object inconsistency over large multi-room trajectories.

The qualitative results are strong. Compared with panorama, video, iterative lifting, and layout-guided baselines, the examples show visibly better multi-view object stability and room-level coherence, especially under close-up rotations where many baselines fail.

The paper includes meaningful ablations. The comparison between depth-only, depth+objects, depth+walls+bboxes, and full mesh conditioning supports the claim that both reconstructed objects and accumulated wall textures contribute to consistency. The 3DGS initialization/depth-loss ablations also isolate the importance of mesh-anchored reconstruction.

The evaluation is broader than many generative scene papers: it includes automatic image quality, a 31-participant perceptual study, cross-view depth reprojection metrics, mesh alignment, scaling/cost analysis from 4 to 12 rooms, and a navigability measure.

The method is described clearly, with useful implementation details in the appendix, including camera sampling, validation, texturing filters, baseline setup, prompt details, and alternative local backbones. This improves reproducibility relative to many large generative-system papers.
weaknesses: The evidence is still somewhat limited for the scale of the claims. Many quantitative results are over only five scenes, the main ablation perceptual study is on a single gothic-revival scene, and the paper claims arbitrarily large or environment-scale generation without demonstrating substantially larger, more diverse, or structurally complex environments.

The pipeline depends heavily on powerful external foundation models and partly proprietary/API components, including Claude Opus, Nano Banana Pro, Flux2-Klein, SAM3, and SAM-3D-Objects. Although a local Flux2-klein path is reported, reproducibility and attribution would be stronger with clearer release plans, exact model versions, seeds, costs, and failure cases.

The object segmentation stage is interactive: users provide point prompts for SAM3 masks. This weakens the text-to-3D automation claim and makes scalability/user effort hard to judge. The suggested automatic alternative is not evaluated.

The baseline comparisons may not be fully balanced. Some baselines are designed for single-room, panorama-centered, or predefined-trajectory settings, while the evaluation emphasizes close-object rotations and multi-room trajectories that are especially favorable to WorldMesh’s scaffold. This is still informative, but the paper should be more explicit about domain mismatch and include stronger controlled comparisons where possible.

The validation metric based on depth-edge recall checks missing scaffold edges but ignores extra hallucinated structures. Since the method allows plausible new content, this design is understandable, but it may miss important geometric violations and overstate structural adherence.

The limitations section is too brief. Important remaining issues include multi-floor generation, manual segmentation effort, dependence on object reconstruction quality, texture seams/occlusion artifacts, physical plausibility of object placement, failure rates beyond retained-view yield, and possible copyright/societal issues from using large image models to synthesize interiors.
